title: Body-wide delivery that alters essentially every malignant cell

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a repeatable systemic delivery method that carries a therapeutic payload through the bloodstream to dispersed solid-tumor deposits and produces its intended effect in essentially every malignant cell, while preserving vital normal tissues. The payload might change gene activity, deliver a drug or initiate a cell program. The defining achievement would be safe, functional coverage across metastatic disease, including poorly accessible regions within individual deposits.

This concept requires distinguishing three measurements: how much administered material accumulates in a tumor, how many malignant cells receive it, and how many of those cells undergo the intended functional change. Material measured in a tumor mass may remain outside malignant cells or enter other cell types. Even intracellular payload presence does not establish adequate biological action. The supplied delivery review treats tumor accumulation, tissue penetration, cellular internalization and retention as separate challenges.

significance.text: The supplied reviews identify delivery as a major obstacle to translating cancer nanomedicines and nucleic-acid therapies into effective treatments. A method that reliably achieved safe functional coverage throughout metastatic solid tumors could make otherwise delivery-limited treatments clinically feasible. Its direct contribution would be to extend effective exposure across the malignant population, including cells protected by unfavorable vascular or tissue environments.

Conditional synthesis: that capability could support widespread tumor killing, disabling a shared malignant dependency or durably reprogramming malignant cells. Delivery alone would not establish any of those outcomes. Each would still require an appropriate payload, susceptibility of the relevant malignant populations, sufficient exposure and persistence of the effect. Activity in cultured cells would not establish these properties in patients, and a small surviving population could still permit recurrence. Near-universal delivery therefore creates an opportunity for eradication rather than guaranteeing it.

Early in-body CAR-T generation illustrates progress in delivering genetic instructions to a therapeutically useful cell population. Its recipient cells are endogenous T cells, which subsequently act against cancer. That is a different achievement from placing a functional payload inside essentially every carcinoma cell. The ESO-T01 report also illustrates why response, persistence and eradication must be assessed separately: initial responses occurred alongside subsequent progression in several patients.

missing_breakthrough.text: The target capability is coordinated transport and functional action across a sequence of barriers: survival during circulation, passage across tumor blood vessels, penetration through tumor tissue, entry into malignant cells and sufficient intracellular retention or activity. Vascular access varies among tumors and within individual deposits. Sparse endothelial gaps, basement membranes and stromal structures can impede transport, so success in one well-perfused tumor region does not establish coverage elsewhere.

Specificity must be maintained while increasing coverage. The supplied review describes off-target interactions involving other cell-surface receptors, illustrating the difficulty of using ligand-directed transport to reach malignant cells while sparing normal tissues. The evidence does not establish that every possible cancer-selective marker is absent, or that one marker could solve delivery across all malignant populations. Marker heterogeneity and normal-tissue exposure remain questions to resolve for any proposed system.

Repeatability is part of the missing capability. A delivery system must sustain adequate exposure over the treatment schedule without unacceptable cumulative toxicity or loss of effectiveness. The nucleic-acid review identifies tumor-microenvironment barriers for both intratumoral and systemic administration and notes that clinical trials commonly involve repeat dosing. The available evidence does not quantify how much each barrier contributes across all delivery platforms or metastatic sites.

current_state.text: The 2024 Nature Communications review, Transvascular transport of nanocarriers for tumor delivery, reports a literature-derived estimate that less than 1% of intravenously injected nanocarriers reach the tumor site in vivo. This is an estimate of tumor-site accumulation, not a measurement of the fraction of malignant cells receiving a payload or undergoing functional alteration. It should not be interpreted as a universal ceiling for every delivery system. The supplied review had complete HTML evidence for this statement and the transport barriers, although figure images were not inspected.

The April 2024 Nature Reviews Clinical Oncology article, Nucleic acid-based drugs for patients with solid tumours, identifies microenvironmental obstacles to both intratumoral and systemically administered nucleic-acid therapies and discusses the relevance of repeat dosing. The supplied assessment had access to the subscription preview's abstract and key points, rather than the full article. The microenvironment-barrier statement occurs in the key points. These accessible portions support the scoped conclusions without establishing the contents of the unavailable main text.

An October 6, 2026 Nature Medicine report describes extended follow-up of four patients with relapsed/refractory myeloma treated with ESO-T01, using a March 2026 data cutoff. Two patients achieved stringent complete responses and two achieved partial responses. Reported median progression-free survival was 4.0 months, with a range of 3.0–15.0 months; one patient maintained a stringent complete response through 15 months of follow-up. Three patients relapsed or progressed. All four experienced cytokine release syndrome and grade 3 or higher hematotoxicities.

These results demonstrate early human activity from in vivo CAR-T generation in a small, uncontrolled myeloma study. They do not establish durable benefit across a broader population, acceptable safety at ordinary clinical scale or near-universal functional delivery into malignant cells throughout metastatic solid tumors. According to the supplied assessment, full HTML supported the reported outcomes despite text-extraction problems in some PDF pages; figure images were not inspected.

The research notes also describe a 2026 Journal of Clinical Oncology conference abstract involving seven people with B-cell lymphoma, CD8-targeted lipid nanoparticles, transient CAR expression and early tumor responses. No source text or captured artifact for that abstract was supplied to the evidence review. Those details therefore remain unverified within this record. The missing evidence does not establish that the reported study or findings are false.

Taken together, the supplied evidence documents delivery barriers, limited tumor-site accumulation estimates and early in-body immune-cell engineering. It does not demonstrate the proposed body-wide malignant-cell coverage capability. The supplied freshness record contains no search coverage, so these dated findings cannot establish the latest field-wide position or prove that the capability remained undemonstrated everywhere as of November 1, 2026.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: after systemic dosing, validated measurements that distinguish individual malignant cells should show functional payload action in a prespecified near-universal fraction across multiple metastatic sites. Measurements should assess spatial heterogeneity, exposure duration and repeat dosing, including regions with unfavorable vascular access. The fraction and duration required should be justified for the payload and disease; no numerical threshold in this proposal is an established completion standard.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed demonstration

completion_criteria.text: Proposed safety and efficacy demonstration: evaluate relevant normal tissues and organ function over an adequate follow-up period, including cumulative effects of repeat dosing. Durable tumor clearance should be accompanied by evidence linking the outcome to malignant-cell coverage and payload action. A negative finding in one normal tissue would provide limited safety evidence, and clinical response alone would not establish the delivery mechanism.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed safety and efficacy demonstration

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: reproduce the result in independent cohorts and, where feasible, independent laboratories, while documenting the tumor types, metastatic sites, payloads, dose schedules and patient characteristics tested. Sampling should explicitly account for detection limits and deposits that cannot be biopsied. Multiple biopsies can establish demonstrated breadth but cannot prove that every malignant cell in every deposit was altered or that every vital tissue was spared. Claims of generality should remain bounded by the systems and populations examined.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries

completion_criteria.text: Bulk tumor accumulation would remain an insufficient endpoint. Delivery of even a few percent of the injected dose to a tumor mass would not establish near-universal malignant-cell alteration. A convincing evaluation must connect transport into the tumor with malignant-cell internalization, functional action, therapeutic outcome and safety. The supplied reviews motivate these distinct endpoints and repeat-dose assessment, but do not prescribe the particular proposed demonstration above.
completion_criteria.label: Bulk tumor accumulation would remain an insufficient endpoint.

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: ONC-04, A shared malignant dependency that renewing normal tissues can spare, concerns what to attack selectively; ONC-06, Stable reversion of carcinoma cells to non-malignant tissue identity, concerns the biological change to induce. ONC-07 concerns reaching malignant cells and producing the chosen payload's effect. Either neighboring advance could benefit from broad delivery, but neither establishes that coverage, and delivery would not establish a shared dependency or stable reversion.

Roster-based synthesis: ONC-05, Therapies that drive the whole clonal population to extinction, overlaps with ONC-07 through the importance of residual malignant cells. ONC-05 requires elimination across malignant clones, including populations that may resist an otherwise well-delivered treatment. ONC-03, Eradication of dormant disseminated tumor cells that cause late relapse, focuses on a particular reservoir of recurrence. Broad delivery might help reach that reservoir, but efficacy in established metastatic deposits would not by itself establish action against dormant disseminated cells.

Roster-based synthesis: ONC-02, Sterilizing immune clearance of established metastatic carcinomas, seeks eradication through immune action. It could overlap with delivery of an immune-modulating payload, but immune clearance does not necessarily require payload entry into every carcinoma cell. ONC-12, Off-the-shelf cell therapy that matches autologous cures and can be given at ordinary scale, concerns cell-therapy performance and availability. Manufacturing cells outside the body and engineering endogenous T cells inside the body are distinct production approaches; neither alone establishes ONC-07's malignant-cell coverage.

Roster-based synthesis: ONC-01, Mortality-reducing detection of lethal cancers while they are still localized, and ONC-10, A reliable distinction between early neoplasms that will kill and those that will not, concern detection and risk discrimination. ONC-11, Real-time, cell-resolution guidance that makes incomplete cancer surgery uncommon, concerns local surgical completeness. These could improve treatment selection or removal of localized disease, while ONC-07 addresses systemic access to malignant cells across dispersed deposits.

Roster-based synthesis: ONC-08, Interception of non-viral precancers before they invade, and ONC-09, Prophylactic immunity that prevents the common non-viral cancers, act earlier in disease development. Delivery technology could contribute to an interception or prevention strategy, but treating disseminated malignancy would not establish prevention of cancer initiation or invasion. These comparisons use the supplied roster titles; detailed specifications for the other concepts were not provided.

change_log.change: Preserved ONC-07's identity while defining success as functional action in essentially every malignant cell across metastatic solid-tumor deposits.
change_log.reason: Payload presence and bulk accumulation are weaker endpoints than the proposed innovation requires.

change_log.change: Expanded the transport explanation to include circulation, extravasation, tissue penetration, internalization, retention and heterogeneous access.
change_log.reason: The reviewed evidence supports a sequence of distinct biological barriers rather than a single tumor-entry problem.

change_log.change: Replaced categorical claims about absent universal cancer markers and generalized liver-and-spleen clearance with a scoped specificity discussion.
change_log.reason: The inspected evidence supports off-target interactions but does not establish those stronger general assertions.

change_log.change: Retained the revolutionary impact argument while making clinical feasibility and eradication conditional on payload action, susceptibility, exposure and durability.
change_log.reason: The supplied evidence does not establish widespread delivery-specific failure across all named payload classes, and culture activity cannot establish clinical eradication.

change_log.change: Preserved the less-than-1% estimate with its literature-derived, tumor-site denominator.
change_log.reason: The estimate is neither a malignant-cell coverage percentage nor a universal transport ceiling.

change_log.change: Preserved all supported ESO-T01 response and progression-free-survival figures, adding the data cutoff, progression events, toxicity and study-design limits.
change_log.reason: The additional context is necessary to interpret early human activity and its durability without overstating the result.

change_log.change: Retained the lymphoma abstract's reported details as unverified within the supplied evidence.
change_log.reason: No captured source text was available; this limits assessment without disproving the report.

change_log.change: Strengthened completion proposals with functional measurements, repeat dosing, broader safety assessment, reproducibility and explicit sampling boundaries.
change_log.reason: Multiple biopsies and one negative normal tissue cannot establish universal coverage or body-wide safety.

change_log.change: Preserved relevant access limitations while relying on the review's adequate HTML evidence for dated findings.
change_log.reason: The nucleic-acid review was only partially accessible, while PDF extraction problems did not invalidate independently supported ESO-T01 results. Regulatory PDFs grouped under the nucleic-acid article were not substitutes for its full text.

change_log.change: Added title-based distinctions across the supplied concept roster without merging entries.
change_log.reason: The roster supports bounded comparisons, although detailed specifications for neighboring concepts remain unavailable.

unresolved_issues: The supplied freshness record is empty; the field-wide latest state and continued absence of the target capability as of November 1, 2026 remain unverified.
The seven-person CD8-targeted lipid-nanoparticle lymphoma report requires source text before its design, numerical results, safety and interpretation can be assessed.

No near-universal coverage threshold, required exposure duration or acceptable residual malignant-cell burden is established by the supplied evidence; these require payload- and disease-specific justification.
How to infer coverage of inaccessible deposits and assess all relevant normal tissues remains an open measurement problem.
The general role of liver-and-spleen binding or clearance and the availability of sufficiently selective markers across malignant populations are not resolved by the inspected evidence.
The nucleic-acid review's main text was unavailable, and figure images in the other reviewed articles were not inspected. Broader conclusions requiring those materials remain unassessed.
Neighboring concepts were supplied as roster titles rather than full records, limiting precise overlap assessment. All substantive review recommendations were adopted within that constraint.
